## Abstract

The concept of free will is hard to define, but crucial to both individual and social life. For centuries people have wondered how freedom is possible in a world ruled by physical determinism; however, reflections on free will have been confined to philosophy until half a century ago, when the topic was also addressed by neuroscience. The first relevant, and now well-known, strand of research on the brain correlates of free will was that pioneered by Libet et al. ([1983](#B74)), which focused on the allegedly unconscious intentions taking place in decisions regarded as free and voluntary. Imagine you are shopping online for a new pair of headphones. There is an array of colors, brands and features to look at. You feel that you can pick any model that you like and are in complete control of your decision. When you finally click the “add to shopping cart” button, you believe that you are doing so out of your own free will.

But what if we told you that while you thought that you were still browsing, your brain activity had already highlighted the headphones you would pick? That idea may not be so far-fetched. Though neuroscientists likely could not predict your choice with 100 percent accuracy, research has demonstrated that some information about your upcoming action is present in brain activity several seconds before you even become conscious of your decision.

As early as the 1960s, studies found that when people perform a simple, spontaneous movement, their brain exhibits a [buildup in neural activity](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00424-016-1852-3)—what neuroscientists call a “readiness potential”—before they move. In 2008 a group of researchers found that some information about an upcoming decision is present in the brain up to [10 seconds in advance](https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.2112), long before people reported making the decision of when or how to act.

After all, if neuroscientists can infer the timing or choice of your movements long before you are consciously aware of your decision, perhaps people are merely puppets, pushed around by neural processes unfolding below the threshold of consciousness.

But as researchers who study volition from both a neuroscientific and philosophical perspective, we believe that there’s still much more to this story. We work with a collaboration of [philosophers and scientists](https://neurophil-freewill.org/people/) to provide more nuanced interpretations—including a better [understanding of the readiness potential](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2021.04.001)—and a more fruitful theoretical framework in which to place them. Let’s start from a commonsense observation: much of what people do each day is arbitrary. We put one foot in front of the other when we start walking. Most of the time, we do not actively deliberate about which leg to put forward first. It doesn’t matter. The same is true for many other actions and choices. They are largely meaningless and irreflective.

Most empirical studies of free will—including Libet’s—have focused on these kinds of arbitrary actions. In such actions, researchers can indeed “read out” our brain activity and trace information about our movements and choices before we even realize we are about to make them. More significant decisions—such as whether to take a job, get married or move to a different country—are infinitely more interesting and complex and are quite consciously made.

## Abstract

The readiness potential (RP), a slow buildup of electrical potential recorded at the scalp using electroencephalography, has been associated with neural activity involved in movement preparation. It became famous thanks to Benjamin Libet (_Brain_ 1983;106:623–642), who used the time difference between the RP and self-reported time of conscious intention to move to argue that we lack free will. The RP’s informativeness about self-generated action and derivatively about free will has prompted continued research on this neural phenomenon. Here, we argue that recent advances in our understanding of the RP, including computational modeling of the phenomenon, call for a reassessment of its relevance for understanding volition and the philosophical problem of free will.

## The Readiness Potential

The **readiness potential (RP)** (see Glossary) _or Bereitschaftspotential_ (BP) is a brain signal linked to voluntary movement. Its existence has been used to argue against the possibility of free will. Originally identified by Kornhuber and Deeke \[[1](#R1)\], the RP emerges from the analysis of electroencephalogram (EEG) data recorded during experimental tasks involving spontaneous or self-paced movements. When EEG traces, recorded during such a task, are **time-locked** to movement onset and averaged together, a slow negative-going electrical potential is evident leading up to movement onset ([Box 1](#BX1)). The RP is prominent at central electrode sites located above mesial motor cortical areas and peaks contralateral to the moving limb. # Neuroscience, Decision-Making, and Free Will: A Contested Debate

The question of whether neuroscience disposes with free will is **one of the most fiercely contested issues in both philosophy and cognitive science.** Below is a summary of the strongest evidence and arguments on both sides.

---

## I. The "Illusionist" Case: Evidence That Brain Decisions Precede Conscious Intention

### 1. Libet (1983) — The Seminal Ready-Potential Study

**The study:** Benjamin Libet and colleagues (H.E. libet et al., *Brain* 106, 623–642, 1983) asked participants to flex their wrist "whenever they felt like it" while watching a clock face. They measured three temporal landmarks on each trial:
- The onset of the **readiness potential (RP or *Bereitschaftspotential*)** — a slow buildup of EEG voltage in the motor cortex (~−550 ms relative to movement).
- The participant's **retrospective report of when they consciously decided to move** (~ W −200 ms.

the "W-time").
-

The RP onset occurred roughly 350–550 ms *before* the reported conscious intention to move.

**Libet's interpretation:** Libet himself concluded that an unconscious neural process initiates the action before conscious will becomes aware of it, suggesting our experience of "deciding" is a post-hoc construction. However, Libet did not deny free will entirely — he argued consciousness retains a **"veto power"** (*free won't*): the ability to suppress the action during the roughly 200-ms window between conscious awareness and actual muscle contraction.

### 2. Soon, Brass, Hayne & Wegner (2008) — fMRI Prediction up to 10 Seconds Before Awareness

**The study:** Christian N. Soon and colleagues (*Nature Neuroscience* 11, 496–498, 2008), using fMRI, scanned participants as they made **free choices between pressing a left or right button**. A support-vector-machine decoder could predict **which button the participant would press from which regions of the prefrontal and parietal cortex up to 7–10 seconds before the subject reported deciding.**

**Why this is powerful:** It extends Libet's finding about *when* decisions occur by also predicting *what* decision will be made — not merely a generic motor preparation signal but the specific abstract content of a choice, encoded in medial frontopolar and posterior cingulate/precuneus regions. This study is frequently cited as strong evidence against an intuitive notion of free will (see also: Soon et al.'s original DOI 10.1038/nn.2112).

### 3. Hayne et al. (2011) — Abstract Intentions Predicted by Brain Activity

**The study:** John D. Y. Haynes and colleagues (*Neuron* 69, 795–804, 2011; PMC3625266) demonstrated that brain activity can encode freely chosen **abstract intentions** (e.g., *deciding whether to call a friend or buy a gift*) several seconds before conscious awareness. Decoding accuracy exceeded chance by approximately 5–7 seconds before the participant's W-time in frontopolar cortex regions.

### 4. Wegner (2002) — The Illusion of Conscious Will (Psychological Evidence)

Daniel Wegner (*The Illusion of Conscious Will*, MIT Press, 2002) synthesized social-psychological experiments showing that people feel conscious agency over outcomes even when their actions have no causal connection to the outcome. This converges with Libet-style neural findings: our experience of deciding may simply be the brain's way of narrating behavior it has already initiated.

### 5. Schurger, Matsuoka & colleagues (2012) — Accumulator Model Reinterpreted RP as "Neural Noise"

Aaron Schurger and colleagues (*PNAS* 109, E352–E357, 2012; doi: 10.1073/pnas.1210467109) presented a **leaky stochastic accumulator model** showing that theRP can be fully explained as the natural statistical tail of random neural noise crossing an action threshold, rather than as a deterministic "decision-making signal." If the RP merely reflects noise, its significance for free will is greatly diminished — it tells us nothing more about decision-making than rolling dice.

---

## II. The "Contestation" Case: Why Neuroscience Does *Not* Disprove Free Will

### 1. Roskies (2010) & Schurger et al. (2021) — The RP Is Not a "Decision Signal"

Adina Roskies (*Nature Reviews Neuroscience* 11, 462–467, 2010; *Philosophical Issues* 20:389–405) and Schurger et al. (*Trends in Cognitive Sciences* 25, 558–570, 2021; PMC8192467; doi: 10.1016/j.tics.202l.04.001) argue several points:
- **Timing fallacy:** An RP onset does not mean a decision has been "made." It may reflect ongoing motor readiness, arousal fluctuations, or task-set preparation — none of which constitute an actual decision.
- **The RP is an averaging artifact:** When you average EEG epochs time-locked to a button press, any random noise fluctuation that approaches the threshold just before movement will produce a systematic-looking negative slope by definition (regression-to-the-mean / post-hoc filtering). The RP does not prove the brain *decided* before consciousness — only that motor cortex was incrementally primed for action.
- **Libet's "veto" is substantive:** Even accepting the RP, Libet left room for free will via conscious suppression during a ~200-ms window. Roskies and others argue this underappreciated power means neuroscience does not eliminate agency.

### 2. Lavazza (2016) — "Explaining Freedom Away" Is Philosophically Questionable

Andrea Lavazza (*Frontiers in Human Neuroscience* 10:262, 2016; PMC4887467) argues that the common interpretation of Libet-style tasks assumes a **specific, arguably flawed, definition of free will** (roughly, "consciousness must initiate action from time zero"), which is then "deflated" by showing that brain activity precedes conscious intention. But if one defines free will compatibilistically (as the capacity for reflective self-control, deliberation, and reason-responsive behavior), neural antecedents are irrelevant to whether an agent is free. Lavazza contends that studies of the RP "bracket" the very feature (conscious deliberation in meaningful contexts) that actually matters to free-will debates.

### 3. Maoz, Mudrik & Gavenas (2019/2023) — Meaningful vs. Meaningless Choices Differ Fundamentally

**The study:** Uri Maoz and colleagues (*eLife* 8:e39787, 2019) asked participants to choose between two charities for a $1,000 donation, manipulating whether the choice was **meaningful** ($1,000 went to the chosen option only) versus **"meaningless"** (both received $500 regardless). They found:
- Meaningless ("arbitrary") choices were accompanied by an RP exactly as in classical Libet studies.
- **Meaningful choices had no RP.** When participants knew the decision really mattered, brain activity looked different — it reflected a deliberative process rather than spontaneous motor preparation.

**Why this matters profoundly:** If neuroscience can only show that *arbitrary* decisions (which most people do not care about free will regarding) are unconscious, while **decisions that actually matter to our concept of free will (meaningful life choices) involve conscious deliberation**, the implicationist studies do not refute free will at all. Lavazza and colleagues argue it is a category error to generalise from wrist-flicks to moral or practical decisions.

### 4. The Philosophical "Compatibility" Response

**Compatibilists** (e.g., Daniel Dennett; Susan Blackmore) argue that free will means **responsiveness to reasons, reflective self-control, and the ability to act according to one's character/values**, not the ability of consciousness to magically initiate action from absolute time zero. From this perspective:
- Neuroscience is fully compatible with a practical notion of free will. Brain activity may unconsciously bias choices, but deliberation in meaningful contexts shapes those values (Maoz et al., 2019).
- Libet-style studies target a concept of free will (*libertarian free will* — an uncaused, consciousness-initiated cause) that no serious philosopher defends. The debate is about whether *compatibilist* free will survives neuroscience; the consensus among philosophers is that it does (Nathan Baker, 2023, *Oxford University Press: Free Will: Philosophers and Neuroscientists in Conversation*; also see various contributions to this volume).

### 5. Methodological Critiques of Libet-Style Experiments

Numerous critics have identified **serious problems with Libet's methods**:
- The W-time is a **retrospective, memory-based report** — notoriously unreliable (Eagleman 2008; Roskies 2010). There is no guarantee it pinpoints the moment of conscious decision accurately.
- The task is **utterly artificial**: participants are told to "do whatever they want" with no deliberative criteria, no stakes, and no guidance. It measures spontaneous motor acts, not decisions at all.
- Libet himself was a dualist whose interpretation assumed a specific philosophical framework that most philosophers today reject.

### 6. Meta-Analyses Show Consistent but Limited Effects

A recent meta-analysis of Libet-style experiments (e.g., *Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews* 2021; ScienceDirect, S0149763421002578) confirms the readiness potential is robust and consistently precedes action — but also emphasizes that its **interval between RP onset and conscious intention varies widely across studies** (from ~200 ms to several seconds), undermining claims of a fixed, decisive temporal gap. The variability in reported W-times suggests that conscious awareness may have played an earlier role than the EEG data alone implies.

## III. Summary Table: Key Studies

| Study | Method | Core Finding | Free-Will Implication |
|-------|--------|-------------|---------------------|
| Libet et al. (1983) | EEG wrist-flexion; reported W-time | RP onset ~350–550 ms before conscious intention | Unconscious initiation of action (Libet proposed "free won't") |
| Soon et al. (2008) | fMRI left/right button choice | Decoder predicted which button 7–10 s before awareness | Decision outcome encoded in brain before consciousness |
| Hayne et al. (2011) | fMRI abstract intentions | Decisions about *what* to intend encoded ~5–7 s before awareness | Content of free choice unconscious long before awareness |
| Schurger et al. (2012) | Computational model; EEG data | RP explained as tail of random neural noise, not a decision signal | RP does not prove "decisions" precede consciousness |
| Maoz et al. (2019) | eLife ERP + money donation paradigm | **No RP for meaningful choices; RP only for meaningless** arbitrary ones | Libet findings don't generalize to real decisions that matter |
| Roskies & Schurger (2021) | Review of computational models | RP is averaging artifact / noise, not a decision marker | Neuroscience should not be used to "explain free will away" |
| Lavazza (2016) | Philosophical analysis | "Deflating" free will depends on assuming the wrong definition | Free will survives any neuroscience that uses a compatibilist account |

## IV. Bottom Line

The conclusion that "free will is an illusion" is **not** a settled scientific finding. It is one interpretation of a body of highly contested evidence, and it faces strong philosophical and empirical pushback:

- **What the neuroscience *does* show:** For trivial, arbitrary motor actions performed on the spur of the moment with no deliberative criteria, neural correlates of action can be detected before we are consciously aware of having decided. This suggests that at least some spontaneous actions are initiated unconsciously — a finding about motor physiology, not metaphysics or ethics.

- **What it does *not* show:** That meaningful choices (about careers, marriage, moral decisions) are unconsciously determined; that the "willing" we experience is literally a fiction; that neuroscience has refuted any concept of free will that matters for responsibility, law, or daily life.

The strongest arguments against the illusionist conclusion come from:
1. The **methodological limitations** of Libet-style tasks (artificiality, memory-based W-time).
2. The **Schurger accumulator model**, which provides a mechanistically plausible alternative explanation of the RP as statistical noise rather than a decision signal.
3. The **Maoz et al. distinction between meaningful and meaningless choices**, showing that no RP accompanies significant decisions in real-world contexts where free will arguably matters most.
4. The **compatibilist philosophical consensus**, which argues that free will means reason-responsiveness and self-control under deliberation — a capacity neuroscience is entirely compatible with, not contrary to.
